say.text: Overheard on the ward: "The TOF murmur is the VSD. In a tet spell more blood shunts right to left, so it gets louder."
Do you buy it?

choices.label: Yes: VSD flow makes the murmur, and shunting amplifies it
No: the murmur follows how tight the obstruction is
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: the sources tie the murmur's prominence to one thing, and it is not the size of a hole.

choices.label: Back to the question

say.text: That is tempting because the VSD is the hole everyone remembers, and a big right-to-left shunt sounds like it should be noisy.
But the murmur is graded by the obstruction: the greater the obstruction, the more prominent the murmur.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the murmur follows the obstruction, not the hole.

choices.label: Try it from another angle

say.text: Same idea, new angle. Two TOF babies are otherwise alike. Which has the more prominent murmur?

choices.label: The one with the bigger VSD
The one with the greater obstruction

say.text: Different route to the same answer. Even a baby who is pink and asymptomatic apart from a loud murmur is a TOF baby: a "pink Tet" with moderate obstruction.
So loudness tells you about the obstruction: the greater the obstruction, the more prominent the murmur. The hole does not set it.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Right. The greater the obstruction, the more prominent the murmur.

choices.label: Next

say.text: So what do you hear? A **harsh systolic ejection** murmur, best at the left mid to upper sternal border, radiating posteriorly.
And the pulmonic component of **S2** is usually inaudible.
Now the twist that breaks the VSD story.

choices.label: Show me

say.text: A TOF toddler is crying, turning bluer: a tet spell. You listen at the sternal border.
What has happened to the murmur?

choices.label: Louder: more blood is shunting right to left
Softer
Unchanged: a VSD murmur is fixed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: with significant obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed. Ask what that leaves to cross the outflow.

choices.label: Back to the question

say.text: Tempting: more shunting feels like more noise, and you may think a VSD makes the sound.
But the source says the opposite: during a tet spell there is a **decrease in the intensity of the murmur**.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember this one: a spell makes the murmur quieter, not louder.

choices.label: Test me in a different form

say.text: A known TOF child is getting bluer, yet the murmur you heard this morning is now quiet.
Best reading?

choices.label: Reassuring: a quieter murmur means milder obstruction
Worrying: a spell can quieten the murmur

say.text: Yes. During a spell the murmur decreases in intensity.
Picture a narrow road: when most blood bypasses the lungs, less goes through the narrow road, so less noise.

choices.label: Next

say.text: A different way in. A quiet murmur sounds like a milder lesion, which is why it fools people. But during a spell the intensity of the murmur decreases.
Picture a narrow road: when most blood bypasses the pulmonary bed, less goes through the narrow road, so less noise. A quiet murmur in a blue child is a warning.

choices.label: Next

say.text: One more belief to test: "Every TOF baby is deeply blue, and how blue depends on the size of the VSD."
What actually decides how blue the child is?

choices.label: The size of the VSD
RVOT resistance compared with systemic vascular resistance
Nothing: every TOF baby is deeply blue
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: the source compares the resistance across the RVOT with the systemic vascular resistance.

choices.label: Back to the question

say.text: Tempting: the VSD is the visible hole and the baby is blue, so it seems linked.
But if the resistance across the RVOT is less than the systemic vascular resistance, the patient is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: colour follows the RVOT resistance versus SVR, not the hole.

choices.label: Try a case instead

say.text: A pink infant with a loud murmur turns out to have TOF. Is that possible?

choices.label: No: TOF is always deeply blue
Yes: moderate obstruction, a pink Tet

say.text: Right. Colour depends on whether RVOT resistance is below systemic resistance. With significant obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta.
Moderate obstruction can leave an infant asymptomatic apart from a loud murmur: a **pink Tet**.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Look at it as a case, not a rule. Infants with moderate RVOT obstruction may be asymptomatic apart from a loud murmur: **pink Tets**.
Cyanosis needs RVOT resistance to beat systemic resistance. If it is lower, the patient is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Last step: what sets off a spell? Pick the true statement.

choices.label: Agitation, pain, anaemia, fever, hypovolaemia and vasodilatation can trigger one
Vasodilatation is protective: lower systemic resistance eases a spell
Only agitation triggers spells; fever and dehydration do not
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: link the earlier idea to this list. Colour depends on RVOT resistance versus systemic resistance, so ask which way a fall in systemic resistance pushes things.

choices.label: Back to the question

say.text: Crying is the classic picture, so it is easy to stop there. But the list is wider: agitation, pain, anaemia, fever, hypovolaemia or peripheral vasodilatation.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Tempting if you think like heart failure, where lowering the load helps. Here it backfires: peripheral vasodilatation is listed as a spell trigger.
Colour follows RVOT resistance against systemic resistance; lowering systemic resistance moves things the wrong way.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: vasodilatation triggers spells, it does not relieve them.

choices.label: Test me in a different form

say.text: A TOF toddler has a fever and is dehydrated, and turns bluer. Fever and hypovolaemia are...

choices.label: Protective, like unloading the heart
Recognised spell triggers

say.text: Yes. Spells can be triggered by agitation, pain, anaemia, fever, hypovolaemia or peripheral vasodilatation.
Take-home: murmur follows obstruction, softens in a spell, and colour follows RVOT versus systemic resistance.
